content.intro: This lesson studies Typing Vue Component Props and Events within TypeScript and Large-Scale Code Organization. The source PDF subtopics are preserved below and connected to an original working-style example.
content.why_it_matters: Types can make component contracts more explicit, but they add tooling and should fit the needs of the project and team.

content_blocks.alt_text: Static types and runtime validation diagram for lesson 110: Typing Vue Component Props and Events. Treat network payloads as runtime values → Use tooling to catch inconsistent assumptions → Validate untrusted data before relying on it

content_blocks.title: The idea in context
content_blocks.text: TypeScript is an optional specialization for larger Vue codebases; the core teaching path and repository files remain JavaScript/JSX. This lesson focuses on Typing Vue Component Props and Events. Start by naming the state, component, browser behavior, or deployment boundary involved; then predict what should change and test the smallest example.

items.title: Type-based defineProps()
items.text: For Type-based defineProps(), document what data enters the component, which events leave it, and where shared content or behavior belongs. Keep props one-way, emit changes rather than mutating parent-owned values, and add slots only when a real composition point is needed.

items.title: Typed event declarations
items.text: For Typed event declarations, document what data enters the component, which events leave it, and where shared content or behavior belongs. Keep props one-way, emit changes rather than mutating parent-owned values, and add slots only when a real composition point is needed.

items.title: Typed defaults
items.text: For Typed defaults, TypeScript is a recommended specialization rather than a prerequisite for the JavaScript path. Use types to make component contracts and external data assumptions explicit, and keep runtime validation for values received from an API.

items.title: Component model typing
items.text: For Component model typing, document what data enters the component, which events leave it, and where shared content or behavior belongs. Keep props one-way, emit changes rather than mutating parent-owned values, and add slots only when a real composition point is needed.

content_blocks.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref } from 'vue'
const count = ref<number>(0)
const props = defineProps<{ label: string }>()
</script>
<template><button>{{ props.label }}: {{ count }}</button></template>
content_blocks.expected_output: The type annotations help the tooling check component contracts; the runtime still receives JavaScript values. This is an optional example, not a new file in this CodeLeaf patch.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use only in a separate TypeScript-enabled Vue project that has compatible Vue language tooling. The CodeLeaf source patch itself adds no .ts/.tsx files.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the initial values or original code, reload the development app/test, and repeat once with a boundary or failure case. Remove temporary logs and test data before committing.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Work through Typing Vue Component Props and Events with a predict–change–verify loop. First state the expected UI or console output. Change only the relevant input/state value, then observe the result. Compare it with the expected output in the code block; if it differs, check the exact file, runtime/version, browser Console, and network response before widening the investigation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Extend the example to include “Typed event declarations”. Keep the same behavior for the ordinary input, then try an empty, invalid, repeated, or failure condition that makes sense for the example. Record the expected result before testing.

items.title: Assuming behavior instead of checking it
items.text: Write down the expected result and reproduce the issue in the smallest possible example; inspect the browser Console and the exact reactive value or request.

items.title: Ignoring an edge case
items.text: Try empty input, a missing item, repeated interaction, a failed request, or unmounting while work is pending; handle the case explicitly.

items.title: Putting every responsibility in one component
items.text: Separate display, reusable logic, API service, and shared state when that boundary makes the behavior easier to test and explain.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember: TypeScript is an optional specialization for larger Vue codebases; the core teaching path and repository files remain JavaScript/JSX. For Typing Vue Component Props and Events, keep the example small, verify the rendered or logged result, and consult the official references when behavior depends on a specific Vue or ecosystem version.

content_blocks.text: TypeScript is an optional specialization from the supplied PDF. The CodeLeaf repository patch remains JavaScript/JSX-only and adds no .ts/.tsx files. A TypeScript snippet is illustrative and requires a separate Vue project with language tooling. Runtime validation is still needed for API data.

content.task: Create a small example for “Typing Vue Component Props and Events” that applies “Type-based defineProps()”, predicts the expected result, and verifies a relevant boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named Vue concept rather than only mentioning it.
The expected output or observable behavior is written down and can be checked locally.
At least one boundary, loading, invalid-input, or failure case is tested or explicitly reasoned about.
The example uses semantic/accessible interaction patterns and does not treat frontend state as authoritative security.
hints: Start with the smallest observable part of “Type-based defineProps()”.
Predict the output before changing one input at a time.
Use the browser Console, Vue DevTools, or the appropriate test runner to isolate a mismatch.

common_mistakes.problem: The example only covers the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real interfaces receive empty values, delayed responses, invalid input, and failed requests.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one realistic edge/failure case and state its expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: The code assumes an API or feature exists in every runtime.
common_mistakes.why: Tool and API support depends on Vue, the build tool, or the chosen SSR/test framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the linked official reference and record the runtime/version assumption.
